messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 46

# The Weight of the Waiting Room

Marcus is a sixty-five-year-old Māori man who has spent most of his working life building things — coordinating teams, managing timelines, solving problems before they become crises. He is good at this. He has always believed that with enough preparation and the right people in the right places, you can control most outcomes. That belief shattered eleven years ago in a pediatric intensive care unit in Auckland, and he has never quite reassembled it.

His daughter Aroha was seven when she was rushed to hospital with bacterial meningitis. What began as what Marcus assumed was a bad flu turned critical within hours. He remembers standing in a corridor while nurses moved with urgent, quiet efficiency around his daughter's small body, and understanding for the first time in his life that he could do absolutely nothing. No plan. No contingency. He was a man whose entire professional identity rested on managing uncertainty, and here was something entirely beyond his reach. Aroha survived, but she spent three weeks in intensive care, and Marcus spent those weeks in a state of suspended terror he has never fully left.

His wife, Hinerangi, died of a stroke four years ago. He speaks of her gently but briefly, as though her loss is a room he can only stand in the doorway of. Since her death, he lives alone in the house they shared in Tauranga, and the silence there has a particular quality he finds difficult to describe.

Aroha is now eighteen and healthy. She is studying in Wellington, and by any measure she is thriving. Marcus knows this. He tracks it carefully — calls her every second day, asks precise questions about her eating and sleep, monitors her Instagram with the focused attention he once gave project risk registers. When she doesn't answer his calls within a few hours, something tightens in his chest that he recognizes as irrational but cannot dismiss. He imagines, in vivid and unwanted detail, the scenarios in which she does not answer because she cannot.

Sleep is difficult. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, his heart already moving fast, arriving conscious mid-fear rather than drifting into it. The images that come are not always memories exactly — sometimes they are composites, his daughter's face overlaid with hospital sounds, the particular blue of the ICU lighting, the moment a doctor placed a hand on his shoulder and he thought it was over. He gets up and makes tea and sits at the kitchen table until the feeling passes, which it usually does, slowly, by dawn.

At work, Marcus functions well in most respects. His colleagues describe him as thorough, steady, experienced. He is all of these things. But he notices that he has become increasingly uncomfortable delegating tasks that involve any element of unpredictability. When a project enters a phase of genuine uncertainty, he finds himself working longer hours, checking in more frequently than necessary, running scenarios in his head at night. His team is patient with him. He is not always patient with himself.

He avoids hospitals when he can. He has not visited a friend in hospital in eleven years. He knows this is not reasonable. He goes anyway, he tells himself, when it truly matters — but so far he has managed to find reasons why it has not truly mattered.

What Marcus finds hardest to articulate is the way the experience changed his relationship with the future itself. He used to be comfortable projecting forward — five-year plans, retirement goals, things to build toward. Now the future feels like a surface he cannot trust his weight on. He loves his daughter with an intensity that sometimes frightens him, and loving her means knowing, in a way he cannot unknow, exactly how quickly everything can change.

He sits in the consulting room with his hands folded in his lap, composed and precise, and says he's not sure why he's here, really. Things are fine. Aroha is fine.

He says it like a man who has been saying it for eleven years and is very, very tired.
